query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the formation and evolution of oxide layers and the resulting microstructural changes, which can lead to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix
generation.intervention: Elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 500-1100 °C, gas environment: oxidizing (air) or reducing (vacuum)
generation.structural_mediator: Oxide layer formation and microstructural evolution
generation.mechanism: Thermally induced oxidation and reduction reactions, leading to the formation of oxide layers and changes in the alloy's microstructure, including grain growth and phase transformations
generation.predicted_outcome: Degradation of the alloy's mechanical properties, potentially leading to catastrophic failure
generation.baseline: As-fabricated alloy with no exposure to elevated temperatures or reactive gases
generation.boundary: Temperature and gas environment conditions beyond which the alloy's degradation accelerates significantly
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms and kinetics of oxide layer formation and microstructural evolution, as well as the critical temperatures and gas environments at which catastrophic failure occurs

falsification_experiment.design: In situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray computed tomography (CT) to observe microstructural evolution during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant microstructural changes or oxide layer formation are observed during elevated-temperature exposure, and the alloy's mechanical properties remain unchanged, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Similarly, ThermoCalc predicts spinel oxide formation at normal atmospheric pressure and 1100 °C temperature. Meanwhile, during HTXRD in air, corundum oxides formed initially at 550 °C, which is different from what ThermoCalc predicted. The formation of corundom (Mn2O3) during the experiment can be explained with the increase in temperature, and the initially formed corundom oxide changed to spinel (Mn3O4) at a higher temperature (950 °C). If considering oxides that form at a higher temperature such as 950, 1000, and 1050 °C, the ThermoCalc-predicted spinel oxide type is the same as the experimentally found spinel oxide. However, ThermoCalc predicts Co as a second major element in the spinel oxide that can form, but during the experiment, spinel oxides contain only Mn, Cr, and Fe (i.e., Mn3O4, MnCr2O4, and Fe3Mn3O8). ThermoCalc’s predicted oxide structure and chemical composition at a high temperature and in ambient air are closer to the experimentally found results than those in the vacuum. Microstructure characterization and composition analyses were carried out by TEM and high-angle annular dark field-STEM (HAADF-STEM), as shown in Fig. 2. The bright-field TEM image in Fig. 2a demonstrates that the alloy is composed of an fcc matrix in which the hcp phase grows in the form of laminate with a thickness ranging from several to several hundred nanometers. High-resolution HAADF-STEM images of the hcp phase were taken along the fcc [110] direction (Fig. 2b), from which the coherent phase boundaries between the fcc and hcp phases can be observed. The interphase plane is represented by the close-packed planes of each structure: (111) for the fcc and (0001) for the hcp phase. No crystal defects, such as dislocations could be observed at these phase boundaries. Compared to other single-phase HEAs, the microstructure of this DP-HEA is significantly more complex. The hcp phase grows in the fcc matrix and, as such, serves to terminate slip planes for dislocation glide, thereby reducing the mean-free path for dislocation glide.
